candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (look at nights and weekends) and the night-nurse viewpoint moved attention from the daytime review where an anticipatory care plan is written to the out-of-hours moment when it is read; 'forecasting' suggested treating the plan as a forecast written for a stranger.
candidates.working_title: Write the care plan for the 3am reader
candidates.core_insight: An anticipatory care plan for a care home resident or housebound person is most useful when an out-of-hours clinician who has never met them can find it and act on it within minutes.
candidates.angle: Plans are written in weekday daytime reviews, but more than two thirds of the hours in a week fall outside GP core hours, when the reader is NHS 24 or NHS 111, an out-of-hours GP or a paramedic. Writing for that reader changes the content: what to do if the person becomes unwell, which treatments they would and would not want, preferred place of care, who to phone, and where the plan is shared (for example the Key Information Summary in Scotland).
candidates.position: Anticipatory care plans should be written for an out-of-hours reader and shared on a record that out-of-hours and ambulance services can open.
claims_needing_evidence: GP core hours are 08:00 to 18:30 Monday to Friday, so more than two thirds of the 168 hours in a week fall outside them (source: GMS contract regulations for England and Scotland; arithmetic check, 52.5 of 168 hours).
In Scotland, the Key Information Summary is visible to NHS 24, out-of-hours services, the Scottish Ambulance Service and hospitals (source: NHS Scotland or Healthcare Improvement Scotland guidance).
In England, shared care records and ReSPECT forms are the main routes by which out-of-hours clinicians see a person's recorded wishes (source: NHS England and Resuscitation Council UK guidance).
A substantial share of emergency admissions from care homes begin outside GP core hours [N to verify] (source: Health Foundation or ambulance service analysis).

Out-of-hours and ambulance clinicians report missing or unclear information about wishes as a reason for taking people to hospital (source: qualitative studies of paramedic or out-of-hours decision-making in care homes).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (an outcome patients value that the routine measure misses) and 'order of events' led to the timing of home care visits, where the recorded visit is complete but the order of the person's day is set by the rota.
candidates.working_title: The visit was on time; the bedtime was not their choice
candidates.core_insight: Home care monitoring usually records whether a visit happened and how long it lasted, while people receiving care also value when they get up and go to bed and who comes, and those are seldom reported.
candidates.angle: The timing of the morning and evening visits decides when a person who needs help can get up, eat, use the toilet and go to bed. A visit can meet every contract measure and still set a bedtime the person would never choose. Control over daily life is asked about in the Adult Social Care Survey in England, but visit-level monitoring does not capture it.
candidates.position: Home care services should record and respond to whether people get up and go to bed at times they choose, alongside punctuality and duration.
claims_needing_evidence: Home care in England is commonly commissioned and monitored by visit time and tasks, often with electronic call monitoring of arrival and departure (source: King's Fund, Homecare Association or academic reports on commissioning).
NICE NG21 recommends that people are involved in planning their care, including the timing of visits, and that visits are long enough to avoid rushing (source: NICE NG21 recommendation text).

The Adult Social Care Survey in England asks people how much control they have over their daily life, and this is reported as an Adult Social Care Outcomes Framework measure (source: NHS England survey documentation).
People receiving home care have reported early evening bedtime visits and rushed visits as problems (source: Equality and Human Rights Commission 2011 inquiry; CQC 2013 home care inspection report).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (reveal what is omitted) with the home care worker viewpoint and 'the last week of life' pointed to who is left off the list when an end-of-life plan is shared.
candidates.working_title: Tell the home care workers the plan
candidates.core_insight: When someone is dying at home with home care, the care workers who visit several times a day need to know what changes to expect, whom to call day and night, and what is already in place, such as a ReSPECT or DNACPR form or just-in-case medicines.
candidates.angle: End-of-life plans are usually shared between the GP, the district nurses, the palliative care team and the family. The home care worker may be the person in the house most often, and studies report that these workers often feel uninformed and unprepared. Without the plan, an expected change such as a person no longer eating, or breathing differently, can lead to a 999 call the person did not want.
candidates.position: With the person's consent, the end-of-life plan and contact numbers should be shared with the home care provider and the workers who visit.
claims_needing_evidence: Home care workers provide much of the personal care for people who die at home with care packages (source: studies or reviews of home care at the end of life).
Studies report that home care workers feel under-informed and under-trained for end-of-life care and are often left out of team communication (source: systematic review or qualitative synthesis).
Uncertainty among care staff about expected changes near death is a reported reason for emergency calls and hospital transfer (source: qualitative studies; ambulance service data).
NICE guidance on end-of-life service delivery recommends sharing information across all services involved in a person's care (source: NICE NG142 text).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (count something nobody counts) and the service manager's year suggested a simple count of different care workers per person; the check found that Sweden already reports one, which gave the post its comparison.
candidates.working_title: How many different people came through the door this fortnight?
candidates.core_insight: The number of different care workers a person sees over two weeks is a simple, countable measure of continuity; Sweden reports one nationally (to verify), and UK services rarely publish anything like it.
candidates.angle: Continuity is what people receiving home care repeatedly say they value, yet UK reporting centres on hours delivered and visits missed. A count of different workers per person is cheap to produce from rota data, easy for families to understand, and anyone can ask for it.
candidates.position: Home care providers and commissioners should count and report how many different workers each person sees; families can ask for the figure now.
claims_needing_evidence: Sweden's National Board of Health and Welfare (Socialstyrelsen) publishes, by municipality, the average number of different home care staff a person meets in a 14-day period (source: Socialstyrelsen open comparisons of care for older people).
The national figure in Sweden is about [N to verify] different staff in 14 days (source: same).
People receiving home care, and NICE guidance, identify continuity of care workers as a priority (source: NICE NG21 and its evidence review; qualitative studies).

There is no routinely published national measure of home care worker continuity in England or Scotland (source: check ASCOF, CQC and Care Inspectorate published measures; state as 'we found none' if confirmed).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (reverse the default assumption) and the kettle turned the default of doing tasks for people into the question of which tasks the person keeps; the physiotherapist viewpoint added the aim of preserving function.
candidates.working_title: Which tasks does the person keep?
candidates.core_insight: In care homes and home care, taking over tasks a person can still do with time or a little help may reduce their remaining abilities, so a care plan should name the tasks the person keeps doing.
candidates.angle: The default in busy care is to do things for people because it is faster and feels kind. Observational research in care homes described a 'dependence-support script', in which staff responded to dependent behaviour with help and gave little response to independent behaviour. Reversing the default means starting each care plan with what the person still does, such as making tea, choosing clothes or washing their face, and giving staff the time to let them do it.
candidates.position: A care plan should list the tasks a person does for themselves, and staffing should allow time for them to keep doing those tasks.
claims_needing_evidence: Observational studies in nursing homes found that staff responded to residents' dependent behaviours with support more often than to independent behaviours (the dependence-support script) (source: Baltes and colleagues, 1980s to 1990s).

Trials of function-focused or restorative care, which train staff to support residents to do tasks themselves, have improved some measures of function (source: trials by Resnick, Galik and colleagues; systematic reviews).
Doing tasks for people who could do them with support is linked with loss of function, sometimes called excess disability (source: reviews of the concept; observational studies).
Time pressure on care staff is reported as a barrier to supporting self-care (source: qualitative studies).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (find the first question worth asking) and the speech and language therapist viewpoint turned a care home visit away from rooms and menus towards access to health professionals.
candidates.working_title: The first question to ask a care home
candidates.core_insight: When choosing a care home, ask how residents see a GP, a dentist and therapists such as physiotherapy, speech and language therapy and dietetics, and how long that usually takes.
candidates.angle: Visits and brochures show rooms, food and activities. Access to health care is harder to see and varies between homes and areas. In England each care home should be aligned with a GP practice network with regular clinical rounds under the Enhanced Health in Care Homes framework, and Scotland has its own framework, so families have a standard to ask about.
candidates.position: Access to health professionals is a fair question to put to any care home before a move, and the answer should be specific.
claims_needing_evidence: In England, since 2020, care homes are aligned with a primary care network, with a named clinical lead and a weekly home round, under the Enhanced Health in Care Homes requirements (source: NHS England framework version 2 and Network Contract DES).
Scotland's healthcare framework for adults living in care homes, My Health, My Care, My Home (2022), sets expectations for access to multidisciplinary care (source: Scottish Government).

Access to therapists for care home residents varies between areas (source: BGS or NHS Benchmarking reports; state only if found).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (change the viewpoint to someone else in the scene), the neighbour viewpoint, 'distance' and 'the first hour' led to the neighbour or relative asked to be the named responder for a personal alarm. A first idea, a neighbour noticing unopened curtains, was dropped because it relied on an invented scene.
candidates.working_title: Who comes to the door when the alarm is pressed?
candidates.core_insight: Many monitored personal alarm services rely on named responders who live nearby, so people with nobody close should ask before signing up whether the service has its own responders.
candidates.angle: The person most likely to need an alarm, someone who lives alone, may be least able to name responders within easy reach. Some councils and providers run their own response teams, sometimes at extra cost; others call family or, failing that, an ambulance. Knowing which applies before a fall is part of choosing the alarm.
candidates.position: People living alone should find out, before signing up, who will actually come when the alarm is pressed; services should offer a response option for people with no nearby responder.
claims_needing_evidence: Many monitored personal alarm services ask users to name responders who can reach the home within a set time (source: council telecare pages; Age UK information; Telecare Services Association).
Some councils and providers offer their own mobile response teams, which may carry a charge (source: council telecare pages).
Among very old people, many who fall alone are unable to get up, and a long time on the floor is linked with serious harm (source: Fleming and Brayne, BMJ 2008).
People who have alarms do not always use them after a fall (source: Fleming and Brayne, BMJ 2008; check).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (apply it to the poorest or most isolated person) with 'timing' and the envelope suggested testing GP access routes, such as the morning phone queue, online forms and posted letters, against someone with no internet, hearing loss and nobody to help.
candidates.working_title: Test every way into the practice on the person with the least help
candidates.core_insight: A GP practice can check its access by trying each route as an older person with no internet, poor hearing and nobody to phone for them would; routes that work for that person work for most people.
candidates.angle: Online forms and a morning telephone queue both favour people with devices, good hearing, time and help. A substantial share of the oldest people do not use the internet, and hearing loss makes telephone triage hard. Healthwatch documented how digitally excluded people struggled with remote GP access.
candidates.position: Every route into general practice should have an equivalent that someone without internet and with hearing loss can use, and practices should test it with patients who rely on it.
claims_needing_evidence: A substantial share of people aged 75 and over in the UK do not use the internet [N to verify] (source: Ofcom Adults' Media Use and Attitudes report or ONS internet users data).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (name the trade-off openly) and the older person's viewpoint in 'the first week' led to the decision between staying at home with care visits and moving into a care home, with both sides set out.
candidates.working_title: Home with visits, or a care home: write both lists
candidates.core_insight: Staying at home with care visits and moving into a care home each give something and take something away, and the older person's own priorities should decide how they are weighed.
candidates.angle: The choice is often framed as safety against independence. Both options carry risks: at home, long hours alone between visits and less help at night; in a care home, the loss of one's own home and routine, a shared timetable, and cost. Naming both lists with the person, rather than for them, respects their right to take risks that others would not.
candidates.position: The decision belongs primarily to the older person; families and professionals should set out what each option gives and takes away, and should not present a care home as automatically the safe choice.
claims_needing_evidence: Home care packages provide visits at set times, so many people receiving home care are alone for most of the day and night [N to verify typical hours of care per week] (source: national home care activity statistics).

Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 a person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision merely because they make an unwise decision; the Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000 has comparable principles (source: statute text).

Studies comparing outcomes for people at home with care and people in care homes are observational and affected by differences between the groups (source: systematic reviews of long-term care settings).
People who pay for their own care home place and people funded by councils face different rules (source: Age UK factsheets).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (qualify a common shortcut), the physiotherapist viewpoint and 'the moment of discharge' pointed to the shortcut from 'not safe to go home' to a permanent care home decision made in an acute bed.
candidates.working_title: Don't decide on a care home at the lowest point
candidates.core_insight: Judging whether someone needs a permanent care home while they are still in an acute hospital bed measures them near their weakest point, and guidance favours assessing long-term needs after a period of recovery outside hospital.
candidates.angle: Function often keeps improving for weeks after an acute illness, so decisions made on the ward reflect the illness as well as the person. Discharge-to-assess models, intermediate care and interim placements exist so that long-term decisions can be made later with the person involved; interim placements can also drift into permanent ones without a planned review.
candidates.position: Where possible, a decision about a permanent move into a care home should be made after a period of recovery and assessment outside the acute hospital, with a set review date for any interim placement.
claims_needing_evidence: Government discharge guidance for England says assessment of long-term needs should normally take place after discharge, once the person has had time to recover (source: DHSC Hospital discharge and community support guidance; check exact wording).
The NHS Continuing Healthcare National Framework says most assessments for continuing healthcare should take place outside acute hospital (source: DHSC National Framework 2022).
Many older people recover some activities of daily living in the weeks and months after hospitalisation for acute illness (source: cohort studies such as Boyd et al. 2008).
Interim care home placements sometimes become permanent without a planned review [N to verify] (source: NHS Benchmarking, ADASS or evaluation reports).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (follow the event over time), 'paperwork' and 'the first week' led to tracing one medicine change from the discharge letter through the care home chart, the GP repeat list and the next pharmacy supply.
candidates.working_title: The tablet stopped in hospital that came back next month
candidates.core_insight: After a hospital stay, a medicine the hospital stopped can reappear weeks later in a care home or at home if the GP repeat list and the next pharmacy order are not updated.
candidates.angle: The discharge letter changes the care home's medicines chart on day one. The repeat prescription list is held on a different system, and the next monthly order may already have been placed. When the new supply arrives, the stopped tablet is in it. Each handover (hospital to home, home to GP, GP to pharmacy) is a separate chance to reconcile the list.
candidates.position: Every discharge with a changed medicine list needs a named person to reconcile the GP repeat list and the next pharmacy order within days.
claims_needing_evidence: Medication errors and discrepancies after discharge from hospital to community settings, including care homes, are common (source: systematic review, e.g. Alqenae et al. 2020).
NICE SC1 recommends medicines reconciliation when a resident moves into or returns to a care home (source: NICE SC1 text).

In England, the NHS Discharge Medicines Service has, since February 2021, allowed hospitals to refer patients to community pharmacy to check medicines after discharge (source: NHS England service specification and regulations).
Care homes commonly order medicines on a monthly cycle ahead of supply (source: NICE SC1 or Specialist Pharmacy Service guidance).
Referral from hospital to community pharmacy after discharge has been associated with fewer readmissions in service evaluations (source: Newcastle transfer of care evaluations; check design).
evidence_leads: NICE SC1 Managing medicines in care homes, 2014

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (change the scale) and the hourglass suggested moving between a population statistic, survival after moving into a nursing home, and the single family reading it.
candidates.working_title: Reading survival figures after a move into a nursing home
candidates.core_insight: Survival figures for people who move into nursing homes are averages across a group with a very wide spread; they do not tell a family how long their relative will live, and figures differ between nursing and residential homes.
candidates.angle: A median means half the group lived longer. The spread runs from weeks to many years. People who move in near the end of life, often straight from hospital, pull the figure down, and residential homes have longer average stays than nursing homes. A family can ask what the figure refers to, and can ask the clinician what they expect for this person.
candidates.position: Population survival figures after care home admission should be explained with their spread and never given to a family as if they were a personal prognosis.
claims_needing_evidence: A UK analysis of care home residents found a median length of stay of about [N to verify] months with a longer mean, showing a skewed distribution (source: Forder and Fernández, PSSRU 2011).
Length of stay is shorter in nursing homes than in residential homes [N to verify] (source: same).
A substantial minority of residents live for several years after moving in [N to verify] (source: same, or registry studies).
Mortality is higher among care home residents than among people of the same age living in the community (source: Shah et al. Age Ageing 2013).
A median is the value that half of the group exceeds (source: definition).

candidates.pause: Families who have searched for this number late at night recognise it.
candidates.gain: How to read the figure, and the question to ask a clinician instead.
candidates.follow: Careful explanations of statistics for the people who have to live with them.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E105 gives hip fracture mortality figures; this is about reading survival figures after care home admission.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (reverse the default assumption) with 'the first week' and 'first impressions' led to the common advice that families stay away while a new resident settles.
candidates.working_title: Settling in: does the family need to stay away?
candidates.core_insight: Families are sometimes advised to stay away for the first days or weeks after a relative moves into a care home; the evidence for this is weak, and families can agree visiting with the person and the home.
candidates.angle: The move into a care home is a major life change, and the person may want familiar faces most in the first days. Visiting is now protected in regulation in England (CQC Regulation 9A) and in Scotland through the Health and Social Care Standards (Anne's Law). Families can ask what a settling-in rule is based on and what the person wants.
candidates.position: The resident's wishes, not a blanket settling-in rule, should decide when family visit after a move into a care home.
claims_needing_evidence: Some care homes advise families not to visit for a period after admission so the resident can settle (source: care home guidance, Alzheimer's Society or Age UK information, surveys of families).
No good-quality evidence shows that staying away improves adjustment after a move into a care home (source: systematic reviews of relocation adjustment; phrase as an evidence gap).
In England, CQC Regulation 9A, in force from April 2024, requires care homes to facilitate visits (source: Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) (Amendment) Regulations 2024).
In Scotland, the Health and Social Care Standards were amended to support visiting, known as Anne's Law (source: Scottish Government and Care Inspectorate; check date and wording).
evidence_leads: Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) (Amendment) Regulations 2024, Regulation 9A; CQC guidance on Regulation 9A

candidates.pause: Families given this advice may not have known they could question it.
candidates.gain: Grounds, backed by regulation, to agree visiting around the person's wishes.
candidates.follow: Posts that help families at moments of transition.

candidates.stimulus_use: A second reversal from the same draw: the paramedic viewpoint and the stopwatch turned the default of 'call an ambulance and wait' after a care home fall into a structured check by trained staff.
candidates.working_title: After a fall in a care home: check, then lift
candidates.core_insight: When a care home resident falls without signs of serious injury, trained staff using a structured check and lifting equipment can help them up safely instead of leaving them on the floor waiting for an ambulance; when the check finds warning signs, they call for help and do not lift.
candidates.angle: Long periods on the floor carry their own harms. Structured post-fall tools developed with ambulance services, such as I STUMBLE, and lifting cushions or chairs let care home staff decide who needs an ambulance and who can be helped up and observed, with the GP told and the cause of the fall looked for afterwards.
candidates.position: Every care home should have trained staff, a structured post-fall check and lifting equipment, with clear rules for when not to lift.
claims_needing_evidence: A long time on the floor after a fall is associated with serious complications and hospital admission (source: Fleming and Brayne 2008; other cohort studies).
The I STUMBLE tool was developed by West Midlands Ambulance Service to help care home staff decide whether to call 999 after a fall (source: ambulance service or NHS publications; confirm the items).
Evaluations of post-fall tools and lifting equipment in care homes report fewer ambulance call-outs or conveyances (source: local evaluations; check design and size).
The world falls guidelines include recommendations on management after a fall (source: Montero-Odasso et al. Age Ageing 2022).
evidence_leads: West Midlands Ambulance Service. I STUMBLE post-fall assessment tool (unsure of date and exact items)
Fleming J, Brayne C. BMJ 2008;337:a2227
Montero-Odasso M et al. World guidelines for falls prevention and management for older adults: a global initiative. Age Ageing 2022;51(9):afac205
NICE NG249 Falls: assessment and prevention in older people and in people 50 and over at higher risk, 2025 (unsure whether it covers the immediate response)
Local NHS or Health Innovation Network evaluations of care home falls response and lifting equipment (unsure)
candidates.opening_line_draft: A care home resident who falls without injury can be checked and helped up by trained staff with lifting equipment, instead of waiting on the floor for an ambulance.
candidates.visual_idea: Flow diagram of a structured post-fall check, with its items copied word for word from the published tool, leading to 'call 999, do not lift' or 'lift with equipment, observe, tell the GP, look for the cause'. Drawn illustration of two care workers using an inflatable lifting cushion with a resident.
candidates.pause: Care home staff and paramedics know the long wait on the floor.
candidates.gain: A model of good practice with a clear rule for when not to lift.
candidates.follow: Posts that show care staff doing skilled work.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E082 (care home falls need a medical look and bone review) covers what happens afterwards; this covers the first hour on the floor. Check for overlap with category C01 (long lies).
candidates.delirium_check: delirium is not the topic; if the published tool lists new confusion as a warning sign, it appears only as one item in the checklist

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (trace a handover between people or services), the home care worker viewpoint and 'the first hour' led to how a care worker's observation of change travels to a nurse or GP.
candidates.working_title: A care worker's observation is clinical information
candidates.core_insight: Care workers who see a person every day often notice early signs of illness, such as eating less, sleeping more or being unlike their usual self, and structured tools help them hand these observations over so that a nurse or GP acts.
candidates.angle: The earliest information about deterioration is often held by the least senior person, who may have the weakest route to a clinician. Tools such as RESTORE2 in England combine 'soft signs', NEWS2 observations and a structured SBARD handover; the US INTERACT programme includes 'Stop and Watch'. Evidence that these tools reduce admissions is mixed, which is a reason to judge them by whether observations are acted on and fed back.
candidates.position: Services should give care workers a structured way to report change and a named person who must respond and report back.
claims_needing_evidence: RESTORE2 combines recognition of soft signs of deterioration, NEWS2 and SBARD handover for care homes, and was developed in West Hampshire (source: RESTORE2 materials; Wessex AHSN).
The INTERACT programme includes a Stop and Watch tool for care assistants to record changes in condition (source: INTERACT publications).

A randomised implementation trial of INTERACT in US nursing homes did not show a significant overall reduction in hospital admissions, with larger effects in homes that engaged more (source: Kane et al. JAMA Intern Med 2017).
Care workers often notice changes before registered staff do (source: qualitative studies; phrase carefully).
evidence_leads: West Hampshire CCG and Wessex AHSN. RESTORE2 (Recognise Early Soft-signs, Take Observations, Respond, Escalate), about 2019 (unsure of date)
Royal College of Physicians. National Early Warning Score (NEWS) 2, 2017

Evaluations of RESTORE2 or soft-signs tools in UK care homes (unsure whether controlled evaluations exist)

candidates.visual_idea: Diagram of the handover chain: care worker notices a soft sign, senior carer or nurse takes observations, structured call to the GP or NHS 111, decision recorded, feedback to the care worker (arrow back). Components labelled to match the RESTORE2 materials.
candidates.pause: Care staff see their observations named as clinical information.
candidates.gain: A model for making those observations lead to action, with a fair note on the evidence.
candidates.follow: Respect for care workers shown through practical detail.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E180 (a fall in eating as an early sign in hospital delirium care) is a hospital point; this concerns handover from care workers in community settings.
candidates.delirium_check: delirium is not the topic; soft-sign lists include new confusion, which would appear only as one listed item

candidates.working_title: Seeing the same GP
candidates.core_insight: Seeing the same GP over time is linked with fewer avoidable hospital admissions and lower mortality in large observational studies, so it is reasonable for an older person with ongoing problems to ask to see the same doctor.
candidates.angle: Continuity is often treated as a preference or a luxury. Studies from England and Norway measured it and found consistent associations with outcomes. They are observational, so they do not prove cause, but the direction is consistent and the request costs little.
candidates.position: Practices should protect continuity with a named clinician for older people with ongoing conditions, and patients are entitled to ask for it.
claims_needing_evidence: In English patients aged 62 to 82, higher continuity of care with a GP was associated with fewer admissions for ambulatory care sensitive conditions (source: Barker, Steventon and Deeny, BMJ 2017).
A systematic review found continuity of care with doctors associated with lower mortality in most included studies (source: Pereira Gray et al. BMJ Open 2018).
In Norway, longer relationships with the same GP were associated with fewer out-of-hours contacts, fewer acute admissions and lower mortality (source: Sandvik et al. Br J Gen Pract 2022).
Continuity of GP care has declined in England in recent years (source: Tammes et al. or other cohort analyses).

Tammes P et al. Continuity of primary care in England: a population-based cohort study. Ann Fam Med 2021 (unsure of journal)

candidates.visual_idea: Evidence card with three rows (England 2017, systematic review 2018, Norway 2022), each giving the population, what was measured and the finding in plain words, with a footer line: 'Observational studies: a link, not proof of cause'.
candidates.pause: Many older people assume that asking for the same doctor is being difficult.
candidates.gain: Evidence behind a simple request, read correctly.
candidates.follow: Evidence explained with its limits stated.

candidates.working_title: Before a tablet goes into the yoghurt
candidates.core_insight: Giving medicines hidden in food or drink to a person who lacks capacity to decide about them needs a capacity assessment, a best-interests decision with the family and prescriber, pharmacist advice for each medicine, a written plan and regular review; the first question is whether each medicine is still needed.
candidates.angle: Covert medication is sometimes right. The practical risks are specific: crushing modified-release or enteric-coated tablets changes how they work, some medicines taste bitter enough to spoil the food, and mixing a dose into a whole meal means a partial dose if the meal is left. A step that is easy to skip is stopping medicines that no longer help, which reduces how much has to be hidden.
candidates.position: Covert administration should never happen without the documented steps, and each medicine should be justified before it is hidden.
claims_needing_evidence: NICE SC1 says covert administration should only happen for residents who lack capacity, after a best-interests decision involving the prescriber, a pharmacist, care staff and family or advocate, with a documented plan and review (source: NICE SC1 text).

In Scotland, the Mental Welfare Commission's good practice guide sets out the steps for covert medication under the Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000, including a treatment certificate (source: MWC guide).
Crushing modified-release or enteric-coated preparations can change drug release and cause harm or loss of effect (source: BNF or UK Medicines Information guidance).
Covert administration occurs in a meaningful share of nursing home residents [N to verify] (source: Kirkevold and Engedal, BMJ 2005, Norway; UK data if available).
evidence_leads: NICE SC1 Managing medicines in care homes, 2014, section on covert administration
Mental Welfare Commission for Scotland. Covert medication: good practice guide, 2017 (check for a later update)
Kirkevold Ø, Engedal K. Concealment of drugs in food and beverages in nursing homes: cross sectional study. BMJ 2005;330:20
Care Quality Commission. Covert administration of medicines (adult social care guidance page)

candidates.opening_line_draft: The first question before giving a medicine covertly is whether the person still needs it.
candidates.visual_idea: Checklist card in order: capacity assessed for this decision; each medicine still needed; best-interests decision recorded with family and prescriber; pharmacist advice for each medicine on how it can be given; written plan in the care record; review date. Checked against NICE SC1 and the MWC guide.
candidates.pause: Care home nurses and GPs meet this decision regularly and may never have seen it taught.
candidates.gain: A sequence to follow and one practical risk to avoid (crushing modified-release tablets).
candidates.follow: Teaching rounds on the practical law and pharmacy of care home medicine.

candidates.working_title: What 'potentially avoidable' admissions from care homes means
candidates.core_insight: Figures for 'potentially avoidable' emergency admissions from care homes are based on diagnosis groups; they show where services could improve, and they give no judgement on whether a particular resident should have gone to hospital.
candidates.angle: The Health Foundation found that a large share of emergency admissions from care homes were for conditions classed as potentially avoidable. That is useful for planning primary care, medicines review and prevention. It becomes harmful if it turns into pressure to keep an individual resident out of hospital when hospital treatment would help them.
candidates.position: Potentially avoidable admission rates are a planning measure and should not be used to discourage the transfer of an individual resident who needs and wants hospital care.
claims_needing_evidence: The Health Foundation's 2019 analysis of care home residents in England found that about [N to verify] in 100 emergency admissions were for conditions classed as potentially avoidable (source: Wolters et al. 2019).

The classification was based on diagnosis groups, such as ambulatory care sensitive conditions and conditions linked to lapses in care, not on review of individual cases (source: same, methods section).
Care home residents had more emergency admissions per person than the general population of the same age [N to verify] (source: same).

candidates.visual_idea: Diagram: all emergency admissions from care homes, sorted by diagnosis group into 'potentially avoidable' and 'other'; beside the first group, three questions for any individual case: could the illness have been prevented, could it have been treated in the home, what did the person want. Numbers only from the verified report.
candidates.pause: Practitioners who hear this figure quoted in meetings get a precise reading of it.
candidates.gain: A way to use the figure for planning without turning it against individual residents.
candidates.follow: Evidence reading that protects fair treatment.

candidates.working_title: The eFI finds people to review
candidates.core_insight: The electronic Frailty Index counts coded problems in a GP record to sort a practice population; because it depends on what has been coded, it finds people to review but should not be recorded or quoted as a diagnosis of frailty without a clinical assessment.
candidates.angle: Since 2017, practices in England have been required to identify frailty, commonly using the eFI. The index counts deficits such as diagnoses, symptoms and disabilities in the record. A person whose falls and care needs were never coded can score low; a person with many coded long-term conditions can score high while managing well. Studies comparing the eFI with clinical frailty measures show only moderate agreement for individuals.
candidates.position: An eFI category should trigger a clinical review and should not stand in the record as a diagnosis of frailty.
claims_needing_evidence: The eFI was developed and validated by Clegg and colleagues using 36 deficits from routine primary care records (source: Clegg et al. Age Ageing 2016).

The GP contract in England since 2017/18 has required practices to identify people aged 65 and over with moderate and severe frailty using an appropriate tool such as the eFI (source: NHS England contract documents).
Agreement between eFI categories and clinical frailty assessments in individuals is moderate at best (source: validation studies such as Brundle et al. 2019 or others).
The eFI score depends on coding completeness (source: method description in Clegg et al. 2016).

candidates.working_title: Parkinson's doses and the care rota
candidates.core_insight: Many Parkinson's medicines need to be taken at set times, and a home care visit schedule or care home medicines round that does not match those times can leave people stiff, slow and at higher risk of falls and swallowing difficulty.
candidates.angle: Hospitals have campaigns on getting Parkinson's medicines on time. In home care and care homes, the dose time can end up set by the rota instead of the prescription. The fixes are specific: schedule visits around dose times, support self-administration where possible, write exact times in the care plan, and ask the specialist team whether the regimen can be simplified.
candidates.position: Care home rounds and home care visits for people with Parkinson's should be arranged around their dose times.
claims_needing_evidence: Parkinson's UK advises that Parkinson's medicines are given within [N to verify] minutes of the prescribed time (source: Parkinson's UK Get It On Time materials).
Late or missed doses of levodopa can worsen movement, stiffness and swallowing (source: NICE NG71; Parkinson's UK; reviews).
NICE guidance on Parkinson's disease addresses timely administration of medicines for people in hospital or care homes (source: NICE NG71; check exact wording).
Home care visit times often do not match Parkinson's dose times (source: Parkinson's UK social care reports or surveys; phrase carefully if not found).

Parkinson's UK. Get It On Time campaign materials and reports (unsure of dates)

Specialist Pharmacy Service. Time-critical medicines guidance (unsure)
Parkinson's UK guidance for care homes and home care providers (unsure)
candidates.opening_line_draft: For many people with Parkinson's, the time a tablet is given affects how well they can move, swallow and walk over the next few hours.
candidates.visual_idea: Clock diagram labelled 'Illustrative example': an inner ring with prescribed Parkinson's dose times and an outer ring with care visit or medicines round times, with the gaps marked. Caption: 'Ask for visit times that match dose times.'
candidates.pause: Families and care staff who have seen someone become stuck before a late dose recognise it.

candidates.follow: Small practical details with large effects.

candidates.working_title: When a blister pack helps, and when it gets in the way
candidates.core_insight: Pharmacy blister packs and dosette boxes help some people take their medicines, but evidence of benefit is limited, some medicines are unsuitable for them and changes mid-month are harder; guidance advises using them to solve a specific problem after assessing why doses are missed.
candidates.angle: Compliance aids are often treated as the standard answer when an older person starts home care or leaves hospital. Other options may fit better: fewer medicines, simpler timing, easy-open containers, large-print labels, reminders, or a care worker giving medicines from original packs. Which option helps depends on why doses are being missed.
candidates.position: A compliance aid should follow an assessment of why doses are being missed and should be one option among several.
claims_needing_evidence: NICE guidance on medicines adherence advises considering multi-compartment compliance aids only to address specific practical problems, noting limited evidence of benefit (source: NICE CG76; check wording).
NICE NG67 on managing medicines for adults receiving social care in the community advises against assuming a compliance aid is the only option (source: NG67; check wording).
The Royal Pharmaceutical Society concluded in 2013 that evidence for compliance aids improving outcomes is limited and recommended individual assessment (source: RPS 2013).
Some medicines are unsuitable for compliance aids, for example those affected by moisture or light, or taken only when needed (source: RPS or Specialist Pharmacy Service guidance).
evidence_leads: NICE CG76 Medicines adherence: involving patients in decisions about prescribed medicines and supporting adherence, 2009 (check recommendation on compliance aids)
NICE NG67 Managing medicines for adults receiving social care in the community, 2017
Royal Pharmaceutical Society. Improving patient outcomes: the better use of multi-compartment compliance aids, 2013
Specialist Pharmacy Service guidance on multi-compartment compliance aids (unsure)
candidates.opening_line_draft: A blister pack sorted by day and time can help some people take their medicines. NICE advises using one to solve a specific problem, after someone has asked why doses are being missed.
candidates.visual_idea: Decision diagram: 'Doses being missed?' then 'Why?', with branches: forgets (reminders, simpler timing, compliance aid); trouble opening packs (easy-open containers, compliance aid); too many tablets (medicines review, stop what no longer helps); prefers not to take one (a conversation); trouble reading labels (large print). candidates.pause: Families who assumed a blister pack was the safe default see the other options.
candidates.gain: A way to match the solution to the reason.
candidates.follow: Balanced decisions about everyday care.

candidates.working_title: The bag that goes to hospital and comes back
candidates.core_insight: A standard transfer bag that goes with a care home resident to hospital, carrying their medicines, their details and personal items such as glasses, hearing aids and dentures, and returns with the discharge information, keeps information and belongings together.
candidates.angle: The Hospital Transfer Pathway, known as the Red Bag, started in Sutton and was promoted across England. Its value for dignity and information is easy to see. Reported reductions in length of stay came from uncontrolled local data, so they should be treated with caution until better evaluated.
candidates.position: Care homes and hospitals should use a standard transfer bag or an equivalent, and claims about shorter stays should be stated with their evidence.
claims_needing_evidence: The Hospital Transfer Pathway (Red Bag) was developed in Sutton as part of NHS England's care home vanguard and promoted nationally in 2018 (source: NHS England quick guide).
The bag contains standard transfer paperwork, medicines and personal items, and returns with the resident and the discharge summary (source: NHS England quick guide).
Reported reductions in hospital length of stay [N to verify] came from local before-and-after data (source: NHS England or Sutton reports; any independent evaluation).
Personal items such as hearing aids, glasses and dentures are sometimes lost during hospital stays or transfers (source: Healthwatch or NHS reports; check).
evidence_leads: NHS England. Hospital Transfer Pathway (Red Bag): quick guide, 2018 (unsure of date)
Improvement Analytics Unit (NHS England and The Health Foundation). Evaluation of the Sutton Homes of Care vanguard, 2018 (unsure whether it assessed the Red Bag)

candidates.working_title: A DNACPR decision is about one treatment
candidates.core_insight: A DNACPR decision covers only whether to attempt CPR if the heart stops; it does not mean a care home resident should not be treated for an infection, seen by a GP or taken to hospital when that would help, and blanket decisions for groups of residents are wrong.
candidates.angle: Early in the COVID-19 pandemic, CQC found that some DNACPR decisions had been made without involving people or their families, and raised concerns about blanket approaches. Joint national guidance says DNACPR applies only to CPR. For care home staff and families, the practical point is that every other treatment decision is made separately, with the person.
candidates.position: Every DNACPR decision should be individual and discussed with the person or those close to them, and should never be read as a limit on other treatment.
claims_needing_evidence: CQC's 2021 review found DNACPR decisions made without involving people or families, and concerns about blanket approaches, early in the pandemic (source: CQC Protect, respect, connect, 2021).

candidates.working_title: What NICE says home care should look like
candidates.core_insight: NICE guidance for England sets out what people receiving home care can expect, including visits long enough to do the work without rushing, visits under half an hour only in specific circumstances, and continuity of care workers.
candidates.angle: People receiving home care, and their families, can use the guidance as a reference when asking for changes. The short-visit rule is specific: visits under 30 minutes only if the worker is known to the person, the visit is part of a wider package, and the time is enough for a specific task or a check that the person is safe and well.
candidates.position: explanatory, no position

NICE NG21 recommends that visits are long enough for the work to be done without compromising quality or dignity, including scheduled travel time between visits (source: NICE NG21).

candidates.working_title: Housebound and missing from the list
candidates.core_insight: People who can no longer get to the surgery can miss routine care such as vaccines, medicine reviews, blood tests and sight tests unless the practice knows they are housebound and arranges care at home.
candidates.angle: Primary care is organised around attendance. Housebound older people have high health needs and are easy to lose from routine recall. Practical routes exist: vaccination at home through the practice or district nurses, NHS sight tests at home for eligible people who are unable to leave home unaccompanied, community dental services, and medicine reviews at home or by phone.
candidates.position: Practices should keep an up-to-date record of housebound patients and plan their routine care at home; people and families can ask to be included.
claims_needing_evidence: Housebound older people have high rates of illness and mortality (source: Ornstein et al. JAMA Intern Med 2015 (US); UK studies if available).
In England, people eligible for an NHS sight test who are unable to leave home unaccompanied because of illness or disability can have it at home (source: NHS website on free eye tests).
Practices and community services arrange flu and other vaccines at home for housebound patients (source: UKHSA or NHS England vaccination programme guidance).
Housebound people are less likely to receive some routine preventive care [N to verify] (source: UK primary care studies; check).

candidates.working_title: Proactive care and the admissions promise
candidates.core_insight: Trials of case management for older people in primary care have not reliably reduced hospital admissions, while some community interventions may help people stay independent, so these services are better judged by function, independence and people's experience.
candidates.angle: Proactive care is often commissioned with the promise of fewer admissions. A meta-analysis of case management found no clear effect on use of secondary care, and a 2024 network meta-analysis of community interventions found limited-certainty evidence that some combinations help people keep living at home. Reading this correctly avoids both overselling the work and abandoning it.
candidates.position: Proactive care for older people in primary care should be evaluated on function, independence and people's experience, and should not be justified by promised reductions in admissions.
claims_needing_evidence: A 2015 systematic review and meta-analysis of case management for at-risk patients in primary care found no significant reduction in secondary care use (source: Stokes et al. PLoS One 2015).

A 2024 BMJ network meta-analysis of community complex interventions for older people found some combinations, including individualised care planning with medication review and follow-up, may help people continue living at home, with limited certainty (source: Crocker et al. BMJ 2024; check certainty grading).
NHS England's proactive care guidance for people with moderate or severe frailty describes aims that include reducing unplanned care (source: NHS England 2023; check wording).

candidates.working_title: Reablement: free for six weeks, and under-studied
candidates.core_insight: Reablement is short-term help at home to relearn everyday tasks after illness or injury; in England it is free for up to six weeks, and although trial evidence is limited, people offered it can ask what goals it will work on and what happens at the end.
candidates.angle: Reablement is widely offered, and a 2016 Cochrane review found only two trials, giving very low certainty evidence. That is a gap in the evidence, which is different from evidence of no benefit; a Norwegian trial reported improvements in people's own chosen activities. The practical consequence for a family is to ask for personal goals and a review at the end.
candidates.position: Reablement should be offered with clear personal goals and reviewed against them, and better trials are needed.
claims_needing_evidence: In England, intermediate care and reablement must be provided free of charge for up to six weeks (source: Care and Support (Charging and Assessment of Resources) Regulations 2014; Care Act statutory guidance).
A 2016 Cochrane review of time-limited home care reablement found two trials and very low certainty evidence (source: Cochrane et al. 2016, CD010825).
A randomised trial in Norway found reablement improved self-rated performance of, and satisfaction with, daily activities (source: Tuntland et al. BMC Geriatrics 2015; check outcomes).
NICE NG74 sets out recommendations for intermediate care including reablement (source: NICE NG74).

candidates.working_title: What good health care in a care home includes
candidates.core_insight: Care home residents benefit from a named GP practice with regular visits, a wider team (nurses, pharmacists, therapists), medicine reviews, planning ahead with residents and support for staff; evaluations of this model found fewer emergency admissions in some areas and not in others.
candidates.angle: The English care home vanguards were evaluated against matched controls. In Rushcliffe, residents had fewer emergency admissions and A&E attendances; other sites showed smaller or no differences. The components are clear, and the effect depends on how they are delivered locally, which is useful for anyone setting up or reviewing a service.
candidates.position: A named GP practice with regular visits and a multidisciplinary team should be standard for every care home, while stating that effects on admissions vary between areas.
claims_needing_evidence: An Improvement Analytics Unit evaluation found that residents of Rushcliffe care homes receiving enhanced support had fewer emergency admissions [N to verify] and A&E attendances than matched controls (source: Lloyd et al. Health Foundation 2017).
Evaluations of other care home vanguard sites found smaller or no differences in some outcomes (source: Improvement Analytics Unit reports, 2018 to 2019; check).

NHS England's Enhanced Health in Care Homes framework specifies components including aligned general practice, a weekly home round, multidisciplinary support, medicines review and personalised care planning (source: NHS England framework version 2, 2020).
